analysis.one_liner: Creates an FTC office to fight identity theft, restricts sales of Social Security numbers and personal data, and requires breach notifications.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2005 and never received a vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an Identity Theft office inside the Federal Trade Commission to help victims recover, and to police companies that collect and sell personal data. It required companies to tell consumers when their unencrypted personal information was breached, limited the sale or transfer of Social Security numbers and other sensitive data, forced 'data merchants' like data brokers to register and follow security rules, and barred displaying Social Security numbers on employee ID cards or posting them publicly. It also set up a national cybersecurity office in the Department of Homeland Security.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose names, Social Security numbers, account numbers, and medical information are bought and sold by data brokers and exposed in breaches. Identity theft victims would get a federal certification usable in place of a police report, plus help restoring their records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose personal data is bought and sold

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Office of Identity Theft at the FTC with a website, toll-free line, and service teams to help victims recover their stolen identities, and issues a victim certification usable in place of a police report everywhere in the US [S2][S3]

Requires companies to notify individuals when their unencrypted sensitive personal information is acquired by an unauthorized party, with civil penalties up to $1,000 per record, enforceable by the FTC or state attorneys general [S3]

Prohibits selling, purchasing, or publicly displaying Social Security numbers in the private sector, bans displaying them on employee ID cards, and bars posting account numbers with names online, with civil penalties [S2][S3]

Requires 'data merchants' that trade in sensitive personal information to register with the FTC office and follow rules on authentication, background-checked access, tracking who viewed records, accuracy, and giving consumers a free annual report on who has accessed their data [S3]

Requires a clear disclosure box on forms warning customers when the information they submit may be sold to unaffiliated third parties, and lets consumers demand deletion of their data after a breach notice [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Businesses whose model depends on collecting, holding, or selling personal data — data brokers, credit bureaus selling information outside full credit reports, and any company gathering sensitive data — would bear compliance costs, registration duties, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per person per violation. Federal taxpayers would fund the new office, authorized at $60 million a year for five years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, credit bureaus, and companies trading personal data

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly: companies must build authentication, tracking, and background-check systems within nine months, and face civil penalties up to $1,000 per individual record per violation, costs that could fall on small businesses and be passed to consumers [S3]

The new FTC office would require appropriations of $60 million per fiscal year, and the bill layers a new regulatory scheme on top of the existing Fair Credit Reporting Act, which the bill expressly preserves, raising questions about overlapping rules for credit bureaus [S3]

Some exceptions are broad: Social Security number sales remain lawful with an individual's written consent, and for fraud-prevention units, law enforcement, and research, with the Attorney General able to authorize more uses by regulation [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are substantial — breach notification, SSN sale bans, victim assistance, and a right to know who has accessed your data — but they come with real compliance burdens and a new $60-million-a-year agency. The bill preserves stronger state laws rather than overriding them. On balance it was aimed squarely at protecting ordinary people at the expense of companies profiting from selling personal data.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Comprehensive Identity Theft Prevention Act in the Senate on April 12, 2005 [S1][S5]
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the only action it ever received [S3][S5]
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4]
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and it received no vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, credit bureaus, and other companies that profit from collecting and selling Americans' personal information were better off — they faced no new restrictions, and the sale of Social Security numbers and consumer data continued as before. Identity theft victims got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and companies selling personal data

for.name: Sen. Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an FTC identity theft office, restrict the sale of Social Security numbers and personal data, and require breach notification.

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Joined Schumer in introducing the bill in the Senate.

for.name: 5 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan-chamber-record support of six Democrats total but none from the majority party.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out, keeping it from any floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled action on the bill, which sat without a vote until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All six Senate supporters — Schumer, Nelson, and five cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Commerce Committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would force them to register with the FTC, follow strict access and accuracy rules, and face penalties up to $1,000 per record for violations — directly cutting into the business of collecting and selling Americans' sensitive personal information. Ordinary people benefit from those same restrictions.

Credit bureaus would have to register and accept restrictions when selling Social Security numbers and other data outside full consumer reports, while full credit reports stayed under the existing Fair Credit Reporting Act. Their business of selling 'credit header' data with SSNs was the bill's specific target.

industries.industry: Companies collecting customer data (retailers, employers, online businesses)
industries.note: Any company gathering sensitive personal information would face breach-notification duties, security requirements, disclosure-box notices on forms, and penalties — compliance costs that could be passed to consumers in exchange for better protection of their data.
